chunks: Ibn Shubrama said: 'I do not recall a hadith I heard from Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) except that it almost pierces my heart. He said: My father narrated to me, from my grandfather, from the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family).'
Ibn Shubrama said: 'And I swear by God, his father did not lie about his grandfather, nor did his grandfather lie about the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family).'

He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: Whoever acts by analogies (qiyas) has been destroyed and has caused destruction, and whoever issues fatwas to the people without knowledge, while he does not know the abrogating verse from the abrogated, and the decisive from the allegorical, has been destroyed and has caused destruction.

key_terms.النَّاسِخَ وَالْمَنْسُوخَ: Abrogating and abrogated verses — foundational Quranic science about which earlier rulings were superseded by later revelations
key_terms.الْمَقَايِيسِ: Qiyas — analogical reasoning used by some jurists to derive rulings; condemned here as a source of error
key_terms.الْمُحْكَمَ وَالْمُتَشَابِهَ: Decisive and allegorical verses (Quran 3:7) — clear unambiguous verses vs. those requiring interpretation

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet say about issuing fatwas without knowledge of Quranic sciences?
ai.summary: This hadith presents the testimony of Ibn Shubrama, a Sunni judge of Kufa, who was so moved by the narrations of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) that they nearly broke his heart. The Imam transmitted a prophetic tradition through his father and grandfather condemning those who engage in analogical reasoning (qiyas) or issue religious rulings without mastering Quranic sciences — specifically the distinction between abrogating and abrogated verses, and decisive versus allegorical verses. This reflects the Shia emphasis on authentic transmitted knowledge over individual reasoning.
